summary.text: Plants can reproduce sexually, by the fusion of gametes, or asexually, with only one parent involved.
Sexual reproduction gives offspring that differ genetically from both parents, while vegetative reproduction gives clones identical to the parent.
Many plants spread vegetatively through parts such as rhizomes, runners, bulbs and tubers.

facts.label: Vegetative offspring
facts.value: Clones, identical to the parent unless mutations occur

facts.label: Main drawback
facts.value: Pathogens can pass from parent to offspring

facts.label: Dandelions
facts.value: Make seeds without fertilization, called apomixis

facts.label: Strawberries
facts.value: Spread by runners, also called stolons

items.prompt: You snip a stem from a spider plant and root it, and it grows into a new plant. How does the new plant compare with the original?

options.label: It is a blend of two parents, like a plant grown from seed
It differs from the original because gametes had to fuse
It is genetically identical, since only one parent is involved
It matches the original only if it is later pollinated

items.explain: A clipping grows into a clone: no gametes fuse and only one parent is involved, so the offspring is genetically identical to the parent.

items.prompt: A gardener buries a potato tuber and a new potato plant grows, with no flowers or pollen involved. What kind of reproduction is this?

options.label: Vegetative reproduction, a form of asexual reproduction
Sexual reproduction, because a new individual forms
Apomixis, because a seed is made without fertilization
Pseudogamy, because pollen starts the new plant

items.explain: Potatoes reproduce vegetatively from underground tubers, which is asexual: new individuals form without the fusion of gametes.

items.prompt: A grower raises a whole orchard from cuttings of one plant that carries an infection. What risk does this method create?

options.label: Every cutting will differ genetically from the parent
The cuttings cannot root without gametes fusing
Each plant will fight off the infection better
The infection can pass from the parent to the new plants

items.explain: A major disadvantage of vegetative reproduction is that pathogens are passed from parent to offspring; this is uncommon with seeds.

items.prompt: A nursery wants every tree to bear the same prized fruit, but seeds from that tree do not give the same fruit. What does it do?

options.label: Plant seeds from the best tree and hope they match
Bud or graft the prized variety onto rootstock
Hand-pollinate the tree again each spring
Wait for the tree to make clones by itself

items.explain: Asexual methods are most often used for varieties that do not come true from seed, and fruit trees are propagated by budding or grafting onto rootstocks.

items.prompt: Over a few growing seasons, one plant spreads across a lawn by underground stems, so the lawn holds many apparent individuals. How are they related?

options.label: They are genetically identical members of one clonal colony
They are siblings, each with a different mix of traits
They grew from separate seeds, so each is unique
They match only the neighbours they touch directly

items.explain: Plants that persist through vegetative reproduction form a clonal colony, and every apparent individual in it is genetically identical to the others.

items.prompt: A dandelion produces seeds even though no embryo was fertilized. How is this best described?

options.label: Sexual reproduction, since seeds always come from fused gametes
Self-pollination, which always joins gametes from one flower
Asexual reproduction by seed, called apomixis
Vegetative reproduction, since no gametes fuse

items.explain: Seeds made by apomixis are a form of asexual reproduction that does not involve fertilization, and dandelions use it. It is distinguished from vegetative reproduction.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to make new plants
paragraphs.text: Plants can reproduce in two broad ways, sexually or asexually. In sexual reproduction, gametes fuse, and the offspring are genetically different from either parent. In asexual reproduction only one parent is involved. One asexual route, vegetative reproduction, makes new plants without any fusion of gametes, so they are clones: genetically identical to the parent and to each other, unless mutations occur.

paragraphs.heading: Clones and seeds without sex
paragraphs.text: Asexual reproduction in plants comes in two basic forms, vegetative reproduction and agamospermy. In vegetative reproduction, a piece of the original plant grows into new individuals, for example by budding or tillering. Apomixis is different: it replaces sexual reproduction and in some cases involves seeds. Some plants form and spread seeds whose embryos never came from fertilization. Dandelions, hawkweeds, some Citrus species and Kentucky blue grass all reproduce this way.

paragraphs.heading: Lasting and spreading
paragraphs.text: Natural vegetative reproduction is found mostly in perennial plants and usually relies on modified stems or roots, and in a few species leaves. Most species that use it do so to carry the plant through from season to season, and often to let it grow larger. A plant that persists this way forms a clonal colony, in which every apparent individual, called a ramet, has the same genes as the rest. Ramets cannot travel far, though branching rhizomes or stolons can cover a wide area within a few growing seasons. One major drawback is that pathogens can pass from parent to offspring, while it is uncommon for them to get into seeds.

paragraphs.heading: Stems, bulbs and tubers
paragraphs.text: Plants use many structures to spread this way. A rhizome is a modified underground stem whose growing tips can separate as new plants, as in iris, couch grass and nettles. Runners, or stolons, are stems that lie flat above ground, used by strawberries and many grasses. Elms and many members of the rose family send up suckers, shoots from an existing root system. Onions, tulips and narcissi split their underground bulbs into more bulbs, potatoes and dahlias grow from tubers, and gladioli and crocuses use corms.

paragraphs.heading: Gemmae
paragraphs.text: Some plants shed gemmae: single cells or masses of cells that break away and grow into clones. They are common in liverworts and mosses, and also appear in the gametophyte generation of some filmy ferns. Some club mosses have them too, as do some higher plants such as species of Drosera.

paragraphs.heading: How gardeners copy plants
paragraphs.text: People mostly grow plants from seed, but they also use asexual methods that build on natural ones, such as cuttings, grafting, layering, division and laboratory tissue cloning. These are chosen above all for cultivars with desirable traits that do not come true from seed. Fruit trees, for example, are often budded or grafted onto rootstocks that are themselves clones. A cutting is a branch cut below an internode from a parent plant and then made to grow roots, often helped by a hormone powder or liquid. Once it has roots and fresh leaves, it is a self-sufficient, genetically identical plant, and blackberries, African violets and verbenas are all grown this way.
